<!-- The Fable judgement on PLAN item 58, answering the curator's question of 2026-10-19: whether a combination of declarations can rebuild, in the flat number tower, what the Working Draft's tower gave an integer raised to a negative power, case by case (an unsigned exponent, a signed computed one, a numeral, a float or rational base); every way the language and the library offer, with its cases, cost and evidence; the least bad mix; and what each way reverses or reads anew among his decisions. Written on `main` at `3f463d3b5`; it measures one thing (section 8) and cites the rest. -->

# The Fable judgement on item 58: can a combination rebuild the tower's power?

**Answer in five lines.** No, not whole. An unsigned exponent and a float or rational base are rebuilt already, by the declarations the library has. A signed computed exponent can be rebuilt by type, as contract R, at R's cost; it rebuilds the Working Draft's rule, which the team's own code and tests never followed, so the premise he took excludes it. A numeral exponent cannot be rebuilt: a numeral's sign never reaches a type on either path, and under walk a numeral has no type of its own until Q-walk, so no overload can split `10^16` from `10^(-16)`. That is the only case the team's tests reach at a negative exponent, so the hole is where the tests are.

**Recommendation and default.** E, as PLAN item 58's default: the integer's own type at every exponent, `IntegerOverflow` where the result is not an integer, `DivisionByZero` at a base of 0, ±1 exact; a float or rational base for a fraction, as the library already does; `fail[\ZZ32\]` in `strToInt`; the three team tests and the two demos written with a float base. It is itself the combination he is looking for, split on the other operand: the base's type says whether a negative exponent has a value, and the sign of the exponent, a value, is tested at run time, as the library tests every such subset (P-80). He can take it without reading on. Nothing in it reverses a decision on record.

Short names: REPORT is `explorations/perf-probes/integer-power/REPORT.md`; the review is `explorations/reviews/integer-power-negative-exponent.md`; the digest is `explorations/reviews/digest-2026-10-19.md`; B.2 is section B.2 of `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-10-19-haiku/fable-judgement.md`; `P-` is a POSITIONS entry, `F-` a FACTS entry, "row" a gap-ledger row; a bare `fss:N` is `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `fsi:N` its api; `Builtin.fss:N` is `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`; the Working Draft is `Specification-1.0-frozen/`.

## 0. Words, for a reader who knows Swift and the JVM

- `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` are `Int32` and `Int64`; `NN32`, `NN64` are `UInt32` and `UInt64`; `ZZ` is a `BigInteger`; `QQ` is an exact fraction of two `ZZ`; `RR64` is a `Double`; `IntLiteral` is the type of a numeral such as `16` before it converts into one of them (F-79; `Builtin.fss:484`).
- **Flat.** None of these is a subtype of another, as Swift's integer types are not. Each wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one, and the conversion is applied for you, but only when no declaration fits the argument as it is (P-74; F-131; `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:474-478`). `Number` is above them all and has no operators of its own (P-43; `fss:380-396`).
- **The tower** is the Working Draft's design, where ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ were subtypes (section 2).
- **Overloading** chooses, among the declarations of one name, the most specific that applies to the arguments. Fortress does this at run time by the arguments' run-time types, as Julia does, besides the checker's static choice (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:298-310`; the `fortress-repo` skill, "Dispatch is on every argument, at run time"). A declaration is chosen by types, never by values.
- **A numeral** has one type on the compiled path, `IntLiteral`, whatever its value (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:468-469`). Under walk it is an `Int`, a `ZZ32` value (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:1635-1637`; `.../evaluator/values/FIntLiteral.java:40-50`; F-74). **Q-walk** is the step that gives walk's numeral the type `IntLiteral`; it waits for the switch-over and is not designed (P-76; `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md:86`; digest, section 5, item 3).
- **The distance** is the count of the compiled checker's errors over the interpreter's library, 34 today, six of them at integer powers (digest, sections 1 and 2; F-241). **The quick pair** is microGPT's walk check, two programs, 7 checks each (the review, "Words used here").
- **E, Z, R, X** are the four contracts of the ask: an error, zero, a rational typed by the exponent, an exponent typed so that it cannot be negative (REPORT, section 3).

## 1. His question, and the three facts the coordinator gave him

His words, as the coordinator cleaned them (the brief holds the raw text):

> I need more context to make an informed decision. This seems like a consequence of flattening the numeric tower, and much of the existing library design depends on this tower. None of the options seem to fit, because it's not a one-size-fits-all kind of solution that can cover all cases. I feel we likely need a combination of several options to rebuild the original behavior of the numeric tower, but at the same time I worry that might not be possible in the current design. I would like Fable to weigh in on this. Can't we somehow use clever overloads to split the negative exponents away from the positive ones? But I guess there's no way to attempt a coercion to NN when the exponents are already ZZ… Before asking Fable: do you see where I am going with this? Is that an unreasonable direction?

The direction is reasonable, and it is the right instinct: split by type. The answer below says which types can carry the split in the flat design (the base's type, and for the exponent only an unsigned width) and which cannot (the sign of a `ZZ32`, and the sign of a numeral). The three facts the coordinator told him are checked:

1. **Overloading picks by the arguments' types, never by their values, on both paths.** Confirmed. The specification dispatches "the declarations that are applicable to that call at run time" by the arguments' dynamic types (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:298-310`); walk dispatches on run-time classes (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/interpreter.md`, "How walk evaluates a program"); the checker on static types. The one place the Working Draft put a value into a type was the numeral: `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`, with the value `v` a static parameter (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-85`). The revival's `IntLiteral` carries none (P-76; `Misc.scala:468-469`).
2. **Nothing converts a `ZZ32` into an `NN32` implicitly.** Confirmed, and stronger than stated. `NN32` declares one coercion, from `IntLiteral` (`Builtin.fss:386`); `NN64` from `NN32` and `IntLiteral` (`fss:911-912`). The explicit conversion, `unsigned(self): NN32` on `ZZ32` (`fss:806`), reinterprets the bits: `unsigned(-1)` is `4294967295`, measured (section 8). And since a coercion is chosen by type, like an overload (`conversions-coercions.tex:474-478`), a declared `ZZ32` to `NN32` coercion could not refuse a negative value either: it would convert it as `unsigned` does. So "attempt a coercion to NN" cannot be a sign test, as he guessed.
3. **R is already a split by type.** Confirmed: an unsigned or numeral exponent gives the base's type and a signed one gives `QQ`, six declarations per integer type (REPORT, section 3.2).

One more point on his premise, "much of the existing library design depends on this tower". It does, in one sense and not in another. The library as the team wrote it rested on the integers being floats: in 2008, `trait Integral extends { StandardTotalOrder[\Integral\], RR64 }`, so the declared `RR64` of every integer power held both the integer of a nonnegative power and the float of a negative one (REPORT, section 6; row 438). It never rested on ℤ ⊂ ℚ for the power: no native ever produced a rational (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:222-231`). The flat tower removed the first (d846e3644, 2026-09-27), and the six sites are the residue (F-241). So the question is which leg of the tower, if any, to put back, and section 2 names the legs.

## 2. What the tower gave, and what it rested on

### 2.1 The Working Draft, case by case

- **An unsigned exponent.** ℕ was a synonym for ℤ≥, the nonnegative integers (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:65`), itself a subtype of ℤ and of ℚ≥ (`:37-38`). ℤ declared `opr ^(self, power: ℕ): ℤ`, "Exponentiation of an integer to a nonnegative integer power produces an integer result" (`:137`; `git show 5a68404fd:Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex`, lines 506-510). The result: an integer.
- **A signed computed exponent.** ℤ's power does not apply to a ℤ exponent. But ℤ extended ℚ (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:195-196`), and ℚ declared `opr ^(self, power: ℤ): ℚ#`, "Exponentiation of a rational number to an integer power produces a rational result", with `x^y = 1/(x^(-y))` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/numbers.tex:344-355`). So `2^n` with `n: ℤ` was a rational, by type, also when `n` held 3. To get an integer back, a program wrote a run-time check: `check≥(self): ℤ≥ throws CastError` (`basic-integers.tex:181-192`, the twelve check methods).
- **A numeral.** A numeral is digits and letters, with no sign (`Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:1053-1080`). A digits-only numeral had the type `NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]` (`literals.tex:83-85`), so `2^3` chose ℤ's power and stayed an integer. `-16` is the prefix operator `-` applied to the numeral `16`, a ℤ, so `10^(-16)` chose ℚ's power and gave the rational 1/10^16; and `7.07 10^(-1)` was ℝ times ℚ, fine because ℚ ⊂ ℝ (`numbers.tex:36-37`).
- **A float or rational base.** ℝ's and ℚ's own powers, at any integer exponent.

### 2.2 The three legs, and where each went

The tower's answer rested on three things, and the revival set each aside by a decision of his:

- **L1, subtyping among the number types**, ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ, so that a ℤ exponent reached ℚ's method and a ℚ result flowed into ℝ code. Gone with the flat tower, by the exclusion rule (P-43).
- **L2, a numeral type that carries its value**, hence its sign. Set aside for the compiler library's `IntLiteral` (P-76, "taken over the specification's unfinished numeral types").
- **L3, sign-refined types with run-time checks**, ℤ≥ and `check≥`; in the later chapter, the refinements are boolean static parameters of one trait, which the exclusion rule refuses, and "the way back is the later chapter's declaration-site variance: each flag a covariant static parameter" (`Specification/advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex:14-31`, `:34-45`). Superseded (P-80: "a program tests such a subset at run time"); their return waits on covariance (P-62; row 404).

### 2.3 The team's later word: the code

The code never ran the Working Draft's rule. The interpreter's library typed every integer power `RR64`, on a tower where every integer was an `RR64`, with natives that answer the integer for a nonnegative exponent and a float for a negative one (REPORT, section 6; `Int.java:222-231`). The compiled prelude typed `ZZ32 ^ ZZ32 : ZZ32`, `NN32 ^ NN32 : NN32` and `NN64 ^ NN64 : NN64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:267`, `:326`, `:385`; `.fss:744`): the exponent's type is the base's, signed where the base is, and the result is the base's type at every exponent; its negative case is the cast of `Math.pow`, 0 (row 523; row 441). Steele's `intToIntPower` is bound nowhere (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java:380-398`). And the team's own tests use a signed computed exponent as an integer: `p = 2^(k-1)` then `p BITOR (p-1)` (`ProjectFortress/library_tests/ShiftTest2.fss:19-20`), `d = 2^n'` compared with a `ZZ32` (`ProjectFortress/tests/zeno.fss:57`), and the library's `strToInt`, `d radix^(n-i)` summed in a `SUM[\ZZ32\]` (`fss:4540-4541`). Under the Working Draft's rule each of these is a rational.

So the later word, which outweighs the earlier text (P-26), is: an integer `^` gives the integer's own type at a signed exponent. That is the premise he took (PLAN item 58; B.2, first point). On the value at a negative exponent the code is silent, as B.2 found: a cast's by-product and an unbound helper are not a position.

## 3. The answer, case by case

| case | the tower gave | the flat design can give | by which way | at what cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. unsigned exponent (`NN32`, `NN64`) | the integer | the integer | any contract; the natives answer it today (REPORT, section 1.1; row 438) | item 58's text, nothing more |
| 2. signed computed exponent (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`) | a rational, by type, also at a nonnegative value | the rational, as R; or the integer with an error or a zero at a negative value (E, Z); or a static refusal (X) | R: `opr ^(self, b:ZZ32):QQ` and two siblings (REPORT, section 3.2) | R: 16 of 26 walk tests fail, the quick pair stops in `strToInt`, Q-walk first, 21 edits, about 32 sites of 34 (section 4.1); and it rebuilds a rule the team's code and tests never followed (section 2.3) |
| 3. numeral exponent (`16`, `-16`) | an integer for `2^3`, a rational for `10^(-16)` | one answer for both: the numeral's sign is not in its type, and under walk the numeral has no type of its own | none in the library; a signed numeral type (section 4.6, F2) plus Q-walk | reverses P-76 in part; waits for Q-walk; even then `RR64 × QQ` has no overload, so the three tests still need a float base (section 4.6) |
| 4. float or rational base | ℝ or ℚ, any exponent | the same, today | `Float`'s and `QQ`'s own `^` (section 4.2) | none |

So the whole cannot be rebuilt. The hole is case 3, and case 3 is where the team's tests are: all 11 negative-exponent sites in walk's suite write a decimal scale as `10^(-k)`, a numeral base to a numeral exponent (REPORT, section 1.3; F-247), and the two demos do the same (`ProjectFortress/demos/BiCGSTAB.fss:211`). Under the interpreter the team ran, those gave a float, by the natives (REPORT, section 1.1), which is neither the Working Draft's rational nor an integer.

## 4. The ways

Each way: the cases it covers and how; its cost in edits, the distance's sites (34 today), the quick pair, the team tests, and whether it waits for Q-walk; its evidence. The site and test figures for E, Z, R and X are the probe's, measured on the tree of 2026-10-16 at distance 49 and carried to today's 34 by subtraction (the review, section 5, lead); none was measured again here, since no way below changes the probe's text.

### 4.1 Overloads on the exponent's type

The types an exponent can have: the five integer types, of which two are unsigned, and `IntLiteral`. An overload can separate an unsigned exponent from a signed one, and a numeral from both. It cannot separate a negative `ZZ32` from a nonnegative one (section 1, fact 1).

- **R**, the Working Draft's split: unsigned and numeral exponents give the base's type, signed ones `QQ` (REPORT, section 3.2). Covers case 2 as the tower did; case 1; case 3 only after Q-walk, and then wrongly for a negative numeral, since the numeral overload is `self^(b.asNN64)` and `asNN64` refuses a negative value with "does not fit" (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/IntLiteral.java:291-296`). Cost: 21 edits, 91 lines in and 29 out; `MultiplicativeRing`'s power at `NN64`, with a natural-power body on `Float`, `FloatLiteral`, `RR32` and `QQ`, or walk refuses the library at load; sites 34 to about 32, with two new ones in `FortressBuiltin` until row 445's api fix; the quick pair stops in `strToInt`, "got arg Ratio"; 10 of 26 walk tests pass; waits for Q-walk (REPORT, section 3.2; the review, section 5.3; F-247).
- **X**, Rust's way: only unsigned and numeral exponents are declared, so `2^e` with `e: ZZ32` is a static error, and every caller with a signed exponent converts it (REPORT, section 3.3). Covers cases 1 and 3; case 2 by refusal. Cost: 23 edits, 57 in and 31 out; the ring's `NN64` power and the four bodies, as R; `strToInt`, `strToFloat`, `Format.fss:95` and `:97` converted; the compiled `ZZ32 ^ ZZ32` and three compiled tests go; sites 34 to about 29, about 28 with `fail[\ZZ32\]`; the quick pair passes; 10 of 26 walk tests pass until Q-walk, 14 of them on "Ambiguous coercion"; waits for Q-walk (REPORT, section 3.3; the review, section 5.4). One cost the probe did not price: the only conversion the library has, `unsigned`, reinterprets the bits, so a caller's `radix^(unsigned(n-i))` at a negative `n-i` computes `radix^4294967295` and raises `IntegerOverflow` (section 8). X moves the sign error from the checker to a misleading overflow at run time wherever a caller converts. A checked conversion, the Working Draft's `check≥` that throws on a negative value (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:185`), is not in the library and would be new text.

### 4.2 Overloads on the base's type

Already there, and the split he is looking for, on the other operand. `Float` declares `opr ^(self, b:AnyIntegral):RR64` and `opr ^(self, b:Number):RR64` (`Builtin.fss:158-161`); `QQ` declares `opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral):QQ`, with its sign test inside (`fss:641-646`). So a float or rational base takes any exponent of any sign: microGPT's own negative power is `10.0^(-5)` (REPORT, section 1.6), and `(2/3)^(-1)` is `3/2`, measured under E (REPORT, section 3.1). Covers case 4 whole. For an integer value that must be raised to a negative power, the program writes a float or rational base, `2.0^(-1)` or `(2/1)^(-1)`. Haskell makes the same split as two operators, `^` for any base at a nonnegative exponent and `^^` for a fractional base at any exponent (the review, section 4.6); Fortress has it in the base's type. Cost: no edit; the three team tests and the two demos write their scale as `10.0^(-k)` under E, Z and X alike (REPORT, section 3.1, "Cost"; the review, section 5). Does not wait for Q-walk.

### 4.3 The numeral's own declarations

Each integer type declares `opr ^(self, b:IntLiteral)` beside its `AnyIntegral` one, today `self^(b.asZZ32)` (`fss:801`; `Builtin.fss:462`, `:554`; F-79). The numeral's sign does not reach this overload: the checker types every `IntLiteralExpr` `IntLiteral` (`Misc.scala:468-469`); the compiled path folds `prefix -` on a literal into a literal of the negated value and the same type before the checker runs (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:152-153`; `.../compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java:137-146`), and does not fold `^` itself (`IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:58-107`); unfolded, `opr -(self): IntLiteral` gives the same type (`Builtin.fss:516`). Under walk the overload is never chosen, since a numeral is an `Int` (F-74). So this way covers case 3 only as a copy of what the signed overload does: the integer under E and Z, a `QQ` under R (and a refusal of a negative numeral by accident, section 4.1). Cost: none now; after Q-walk, its body must agree with the signed one. Waits for Q-walk to matter at all.

### 4.4 The witness `typecase`, `cast`, and the run-time sign test

The library chooses by a type with `typecase`: by a static argument alone, through the witness `__thrower[\T\]` and `cast[\T\]` (`additiveIdentity`, `fss:3362-3377`; `cast`, `fss:33-37`), or by a value's run-time type over the comprised integer types (`exactValue`, `fss:398-408`; `Number`'s `=`, `fss:386-395`). Inside an arm, a sign is tested by comparison, which is the library's rule for a sign-refined subset (P-80): `QQ`'s power tests `-other > 0` (`fss:642`), the probe's `QQ` body tests `e < 0` inside each signed arm (REPORT, section 4), and the natives test `exp < 0` (`Int.java:226`). These devices give a sign-dependent value, not a sign-dependent type: the checker types a `typecase` as the join of its arms (REPORT, section 4), which for a `ZZ32` arm and a `QQ` arm is `Number`, which has no operators (section 4.5). Covers: the negative branch of E and Z, and `QQ`'s body, 4 of the 6 sites, 8 lines for 6. Does not wait for Q-walk. This is the way E and Z are built (REPORT, sections 3.1 and 4).

### 4.5 A result type wider than the base

- **`Number`**, the team's first design: until 2008-05-08 the powers answered `Number` (REPORT, section 6). On the flat tower `Number` declares `asFloat` and `=` and nothing else (`fss:380-396`; P-43), so every arithmetic use of a power would need a `cast` or `typecase`, and `strToInt`'s `SUM[\ZZ32\]` would be refused. By reading, it adds sites rather than clearing them. Not measured.
- **`QQ` at every exponent**: exact, holds 8 and 1/2 both, drops the premise; `2^3` is `8 : QQ` (REPORT, section 8, "R's shape"); every failure of R and more.
- **`RR64`**, today's text, the team's 2008 choice when integers were floats: holds neither every `ZZ64` (P-74 keeps `ZZ64` into `RR64` explicit as lossy, P-66) nor the integer the natives answer (row 438); it is the six sites.
- **`ZZ64` or `ZZ` for a `ZZ32` base** holds `2^31` but not `2^(-1)`: no bearing on the sign.

None covers a case the others do not, and each costs more than E. None waits for Q-walk.

### 4.6 A sign-refined type brought forward in part

Three partial forms, from the narrowest:

- **F1, the unsigned widths as the exponent's type.** `NN32` and `NN64` are the only types in the flat library whose every value is nonnegative, and they carry it in the run-time object (`FNN32`), so both paths can dispatch on them. That is X (section 4.1). It reverses nothing.
- **F2, a nonnegative numeral type.** A digits-only numeral gets a type of its own, the Working Draft's `NaturalNumeral` in some form, and `-16` keeps `IntLiteral`. It is the only way to make case 3's sign reach a type. It needs the checker's literal typing changed (`Misc.scala:468-469`), the folder to give a folded negative literal the signed type (`IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:152-153`), a second numeral object in the library beside `IntLiteral` (`Builtin.fss:484`), and Q-walk first, since walk has no numeral type at all. What it buys: under E, nothing a program can see, since E already gives the integer for `10^16` and an error for `10^(-16)`; under R, the Working Draft's case 3, `10^16` an integer and `10^(-16)` a rational. Even then `compoundArray`'s `7.07 10^(-1)` fails, since `RR64 × QQ` has no overload (REPORT, section 3.2) and a lossy `QQ` into `RR64` conversion is explicit by P-74. It reverses P-76 in part: the specification's numeral types, which P-76 set aside as unfinished, come back for the sign.
- **F3, a nonnegative subtype of a signed type**, `ZZ32≥ extends ZZ32`. The exclusion rule allows it, since it inherits `Integral[\ZZ32\]` and no second instantiation. But a value's run-time type is its object's, and both paths dispatch on it (section 1, fact 1); `ZZ32` comprises the one object `Int` (`fss:729`). The team's folder refuses one negative-literal operation at compile time, a factorial, with a `CompilerError` (`IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:38-40`), but it does not fold `^`, and that refusal is a compiler's internal error, not a Fortress error; walk would have no such check. The mix: E's contract for an integer base (section 4.7's two exceptions, inside the run-time sign test of section 4.4), the float and rational bases for a fraction (section 4.2), `fail[\ZZ32\]` in `strToInt` (row 747), and the three team tests and two demos written with a float base. 1. **The team's later word** (P-26) gives the type: an integer `^` has the integer's type at a signed exponent (section 2.3), so R is out; a numeral's type is `IntLiteral` (P-76), so case 3 cannot split; the tower is flat (P-43), so no `QQ` result flows into float code. It is silent on the value (B.2).
2. **The library as the team wrote it** gives the value's shape: it tests a sign inside a body by comparison (`fss:642`; P-80), raises `IntegerOverflow` for a result the width cannot hold (`PowChooseLcmRungE.fss:58`; P-73), and gives a fraction from a float or rational base (`Builtin.fss:160`; `fss:641`). 3. **The peers**, where the first two are silent, between an error and a zero: Julia, Java's `BigInteger.pow` and Haskell's `^` raise; Rust types the exponent unsigned; X10 answers a float; none answers 0 (the review, section 4). It reverses nothing, but F3's form of it reads P-80 anew and takes P-62's work early.
- **If he wants R**: it sets aside the premise he took under P-26, the compiled prelude's integer type at a signed exponent, for the Working Draft's earlier text, and waits for Q-walk.

## 8. What I measured

One thing, since no way above changes the probe's measured text: what walk's `unsigned` does to a negative exponent, which prices X's conversion (section 4.1) and fact 2 (section 1). The probe `ProbeUnsignedPower.fss`, in the scratchpad, run under `nice -n 19` with the skill's setup lines on `main` at `3f463d3b5`, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, one JVM:

```

unsigned(-1) > unsigned(0) = true
2^unsigned(-1) overflows = true
2^(-1) today = 0.5
```

The third line is `overflows(fn () => two^u)` with `two: ZZ32 = 2` and `u = unsigned(m1)`, `m1: ZZ32 = -1`, in the shape of `PowChooseLcmRungE.fss:6-12`. The fourth is on record already (REPORT, section 1.1). The native is `ZZ32$ToNN32`, `f(int x) { return x; }` into `FNN32.make` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/ZZ32.java:54-60`, `:213-216`).

content.text:
The Fable judgement on item 58 is in, so ask 2 comes back to you now in its new form. Ask 3 follows after your answer.

**Ask 2: what should an integer raised to a negative power give, now that Fable has weighed your idea of a combination?**

**Context**
- `2^3` is 8, but `2^(-1)` is 1/2, and no integer type can hold that. In the old nested tower every integer was also a rational, so 1/2 had somewhere to go. The flat tower took that away. Today every integer `^` is declared to return `RR64`, a leftover from 2008, when integers were also floats. That gives 6 of the 34 errors in the distance, the checker's errors on the interpreter's library that must reach zero before the switch-over. So the switch-over needs this answer.
- Fable took your idea case by case: split negative exponents from positive ones with overloads.
  - **Unsigned exponent** (`NN32`, `NN64`): already split. It can't be negative, so the result is an integer.
  - **Float or rational base:** already split, on the base. `2.0^(-1)` is 0.5 and `(2/1)^(-1)` is 1/2 today. microGPT's one negative power, `10.0^(-5)`, is this case.
  - **Signed exponent computed at run time** (`n: ZZ32`): overloads pick by type, never by value, so a negative `n` looks the same as a positive one. The only split by type is the old draft's: every signed exponent gives a rational, even `2^3`. The team's later code never did that. The compiled library returns a `ZZ32` for `ZZ32 ^ ZZ32`, and `strToInt` and two team tests use `2^n` as an integer.
  - **Numeral exponent** (`10^(-16)`): no split is possible. `-16` is minus applied to the numeral 16, and both have the same type on both paths, so no overload sees the sign. This is the case the team tests hit: all 11 negative powers in walk's suite are `10^(-k)`.
  - **Your guess about converting to `NN` was right.** Nothing converts a `ZZ32` to an `NN32` for you. The explicit `unsigned(-1)` gives 4,294,967,295, and Fable measured `2^unsigned(-1)` raising an overflow instead of a sign error.
- So the combination you were after exists, but it splits on the base, not the exponent. The base's type says whether a fraction is possible. The exponent's sign is tested at run time inside the body, the way the library tests a sign everywhere since you set aside the sign-refined types.

**Options**
1. **An error at a negative exponent, with the fraction coming from the base (E).**
   - What it does: each integer `^` returns its own type. A negative exponent raises `IntegerOverflow`, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and bases 1 and -1 give their exact power. A program that wants 1/2 writes `2.0^(-1)`.
   - What else changes: three team tests and two demos change `10^(-k)` to `10.0^(-k)`, and `strToInt` gets a typed `fail`.
   - Cost: 15 library edits. The distance goes from 34 to about 28. microGPT's quick check passes with every value equal. Nothing has to be built first.
2. **Zero at a negative exponent (Z).** As in 1, but `2^(-1)` gives 0, which is what the compiled path does today by accident. Six printed values in a team test change, and no peer language does this.
3. **A rational for any signed exponent (R).** This is the old draft's rule: `2^n` gives a `QQ` even at `n = 3`. It sets aside the team's later word that you took as the premise. 16 of 26 walk tests fail, microGPT's quick check stops in `strToInt`, and it waits for walk to get a numeral type, a step after the switch-over that has no design yet.
4. **Unsigned exponents only (X).** `2^n` with `n: ZZ32` becomes a compile error, so callers must convert. It also waits for walk's numeral type, and since `unsigned` turns -1 into a huge number, a negative exponent would surface as an overflow.
5. **A numeral type that carries its sign, on top of 1 or 3.** It's the only way to split `10^16` from `10^(-16)`. It partly reverses your decision that every numeral has the one type `IntLiteral`, and it also waits for walk's numeral type. On top of 1, no program would see a difference.

**How they weigh**
- 1 keeps the integer type the team's later code gives. It follows the library's own sign tests and overflow rule and needs nothing new. What it gives up: `2^(-1)` has no value when the 2 is an integer.
- 2 gives a value, but a wrong one, and silently.
- 3 restores the old draft's exact answer, at the cost of microGPT's check and every integer use of `2^n`, and it waits.
- 4 is Rust's way. It moves the sign problem to every caller, and it waits.
- 5 changes nothing visible on top of 1.

The full argument: [integer-power-fable-judgement.md](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/reviews/integer-power-fable-judgement.md).

**Recommendation:** 1. It's the combination you were looking for, split on the base instead of the exponent.

No. The cold reads weren't Haiku, and they read only the changed text, so there's nothing to revert.

- **Model.** Both cold reads ran on Opus. They started at 22:59 UTC on 2026-10-19 (00:59 your time), after the Haiku window had ended at 21:04 UTC. Every cold read since 2026-10-08 ran on Opus, 11 in all, and none ran during the window. The skill writer that made the fixes is pinned to Opus by its launch script. Its replies, during the window and after it, are all Opus.
- **Scope.** Each read covered only what the writer had changed. The `fortress-repo` read covered about 108 added lines in three parts, and all 46 of its flags fall on those lines. The other read covered the hooks and the two rules, about 29 added lines, and gave 21 flags.

c302e4613 Item 58: the Fable judgement on a combination that rebuilds the tower's power, as returned, and its INDEX line
## 5. How it is run

The batch runs on the workflow of batch 18: `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`, its manual `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`, and the practice they build, `coordinator/process-engineering/batch-redesign.md`. Each rung's worker does its rung test first; a checker rung times the count stage before and after its change and makes its speed pass; its skeptic checks it, times the count stage itself where the rung changes the checker, and fixes what it finds, test first; a judge rules only on a fix the skeptic marks contested, on a rung the skeptic refuses, or on a worker's stop; the gather lands the rungs on `main` and folds their record lines and their ledger rows through `coordinator/tools/ledger.py`; the merged-diff review and the gate run side by side; the commit stage lands the gate's tables, runs the quick microGPT walk check and pushes. The batch writes no skill text. Section 3 is each worker's brief word for word; this section holds the rest of the manifest, which `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-19/manifest/gen19.py` reads with the briefings of `lists19.py` beside it, and `check19.js` checks.

### The generator

`plan-19/manifest/` is committed with this record: `gen19.py`, `lists19.py` and `check19.js`, made from `plan-18/manifest/`. Changed from batch 18's: the batch's values; the two rungs P and S; `check19.js` checks that no rung declares `landsOnlyWith`, that P states P-148 and the count stage, and that S states the distance stage and the count stage. On `ce752ed20`: `lists19.py`, 48 briefing keys, every one matching one place, 0 problems; `gen19.py`, then `check19.js` on a scratch copy of the script, 0 problems; `workflow-scenarios.js` on the spliced scratch copy, 0 problems. The tracked script is not spliced: the coordinator splices it ("Before the launch", step 2).

### The manifest, rung by rung

Each block gives the fields of one rung's manifest entry. "Its test is the stage" means the checker count or the distance is the rung's failing-then-passing test; no rung here has that, since each has a test file first. "Joins the gate" names a step the gate gains once the rung lands; none does, and `ant testSpecData` runs because 18's landed summary has it. No rung declares a checker count: it is reported, never red. The expected minutes order the scatter only. The points to report are the kinds of change the curator reviews after the landing: a rung that reaches one finishes, lists it with its evidence, and lands; only a step that cannot be undone, or that would act against a decision of the curator, holds the push.

1. The script, this manual and the batch's manifest generator on `main`. The base is `main`'s head after them, by its full hash, passed as `args.base`.
2. The batch's one base build, a worktree at the base outside the main tree, built once and then left alone. Every rung worktree is seeded from it, and the old code runs from it (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The workflow"). About 200 s, as the skill's `worktrees.md`, "Finding or building a base build", gives it:

        git -C /home/user/fortress worktree add --detach /home/user/fortress-base<N> <base>
        cd /home/user/fortress-base<N>      # then set up the call as the skill's build-and-caches.md says
        ant compileAll                      # BUILD SUCCESSFUL
        # the library order (build-and-caches.md, "The library order"), then one walk run, which warms walk's caches:
        bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
        git status --porcelain              # empty: the seed refuses a base build that is not clean

   Its path goes to the launch as `args.baseBuild`. The script refuses to start without it (scenario B1).
3. One trial seed proves the base build, about 3 s: `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh /home/user/fortress-base<N> /home/user/fortress-seedcheck - <base>`, then `git -C /home/user/fortress worktree remove /home/user/fortress-seedcheck`. One `old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base<N> /home/user/fortress-seedcheck-caches ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss`, run from the main tree, proves the old code runs; its folder is removed after.
4. The briefings checked on the base (`python3 explorations/compile-ladder/plan-<N>/manifest/lists<N>.py`). The block generated (`gen<N>.py`), checked in a scratch copy and spliced (`check<N>.js`, then `check<N>.js --write`). Then `node explorations/coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js` on the spliced script, which also checks that every skill section the script cites by name is a heading of the skill. Then the commit.
5. `df -h /` against one seeded worktree per rung (about 206 MB each) and the base build. `git status --porcelain` empty in the main tree, and no other agent writing there or pushing `main` while the run gathers and commits. The session's permission rules let the commit stage run `tools/mg-run.sh`.
6. Check-ins armed for the run's length, 45 minutes apart (the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`, "Watching a run").

The launch: `Workflow({scriptPath: 'explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js', args: {base: '<full hash>', baseBuild: '/home/user/fortress-base<N>'}})`. The args are kept byte for byte, since a resume needs them. The base build stays until the coordinator removes it after the landing.

== .claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/build-and-caches.md:73-95

## The library order

The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.

Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:

- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.

Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:

    cd ProjectFortress
    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s

Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.

- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.

content.content:
## Watching a run

- If you launch a long or large run outside a batch, such as a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour, write its estimate of tokens written in the boot note. A probe can write ten times its estimate.
- Watch its spend: `spend.py <since-epoch> <path>`, where the path is the session's `subagents/` folder for agents, or the project's folder for headless sessions. If it passes the estimate, give the worker an instruction or end it. Watch no other run this way.
- When an overnight or long run starts, arm its check-ins: `send_later` reminders 45 minutes apart, in one turn (`cloud-container`, its stops part). An hourly check-in would let the cache expire.
- Keep each wait of yours under an hour. The `Monitor` tool can watch a run.
- If a worker waits on the curator between tasks, run it as a headless session and resume it within the hour (`--resume <id>`).

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/cloud-container

# The cloud container

**container**
: Virtual machine with its own disk, on which a cloud session of Claude Code runs. It holds a clone of the branch that the session was created from.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**main session**
: Top-level session of a container, which the curator talks to. The agents that it launches are not main sessions.

**coordinating session**
: Main session that keeps the project's files under `explorations/coordinator/` and launches the workers.

**process stop**
: End of the session's Claude Code process, by the platform's cap, by idleness or by a VM restart. The platform starts the process again in the same session.

**VM restart**
: Restart of the container's machine under a live session.

**check-in**
: One-shot reminder, armed with `send_later`, that wakes the main session with a message at a set time.

**Stop hook**
: Command that Claude Code runs at the end of every turn of the main session.

The platform stops the session's process about every 13 hours and when the session goes idle. It can restart the VM, sometimes with the disk rolled back, and it can lose the container. Running agents survive none of these.

## Rules for every agent

- Before a long run, read the room left on the disk as `references/machine.md` says.
- If your brief lets you push, push your work as you go, as `fortress-repo`'s `references/committing.md` says. Only what is pushed survives a rollback of the disk or a lost container.
- After a process stop, a VM restart or a lost container, run `git status` and `git log origin/<branch>..<branch>` in each tree that you work in, before you start anything again.
- The platform's git-check Stop hook can still ask the main session to commit and push on a turn that the git-check switch misses (`references/hooks.md`). Treat its reminders as advisory. Never commit or push unready work to answer one.

## The parts

- `references/machine.md`, for every agent: the machine, timings across sessions, agents at once, the disk allowance and a full disk, the blocked hosts.
- `references/stops.md`, for every agent: the kinds of process stop and their signs, a disk rolled back, the weekly usage limit, what a stop keeps here. Its section on check-ins is for the coordinating session.
- `references/hooks.md`, for the coordinating session: the transcript backup and its blind spots, the git-check hook and how it is turned off.
- `references/container-loss.md`, for the coordinating session: re-provisioning, re-arming the backup, reading another session's transcript, recovering the work.

How a Claude Code session behaves anywhere (the Bash tool, long commands, waits and the prompt cache, interrupts, the automatic permission check) is `fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md`. Running agents and resuming a run are the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

content.content:
## What an entry is

An entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: the fact as it stands now; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; the test that gates it, or its source; the decision it builds, by number; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; what it means for the work; and what is still to build, with its PLAN item. It lists no FACTS entries: `P-48+` finds them.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## Reading and writing

- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

## What an entry is

An entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: the fact as it stands now; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; the test that gates it, or its source; the decision it builds, by number; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; what it means for the work; and what is still to build, with its PLAN item. It lists no FACTS entries: `P-48+` finds them.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## Reading and writing

- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

The width, decision D and decision A clear no site of the 94. Decision D is the model's text (C4), which the distance does not check. Decision A, as A1, rewrites the factories' bodies (`array1`, `vector`, `matrix`). Two of those lines carry fork 2's untraced bound errors (`:2455`, `:2816`); whether A1 moves them is not known.

### None of the six: 28

- **Bodies typed by the parent trait, 13.** `Vector`'s and `Matrix`'s bodies answer `Array1` or `Array2`, because `map`, `ivmap`, `fill` and `tabulate` are declared on the parent: "Function body has type Array1[\T,0,s0\], but declared return type is Vector[\T,s0\]" (`:2396`, `:2398`, `:2399`, `:2402`, `:2457`, `:2459`, `:2752`, `:2757`; for `Matrix`, `:2704`, `:2706`, `:2707`, `:2708`, `:2819`).
  - The measured 6c left them, and it uncovered one more at `:2400` (`sites-RINGVM-vs-L0.txt` at `fb10482ba`).
  - The library's own way covers `fill` and `tabulate`: `ImmutableArray1` redeclares both at its own type (api `FortressLibrary.fsi:1567-1568`, bodies `FortressLibrary.fss:2276-2283`). POSITIONS, "`fill` takes a value, `tabulate` a function", says the same of the leaf traits.
  - For `map[\R\]` and `ivmap[\R\]` the `R` is unbounded, so `Vector[\R\]` cannot be their result. The ways there are a body built through `tabulate`, or a `cast`.
  - No row names these sites. They need a list of ways.
- **A size tested in a branch, 3.** `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => r` and `if b0=0 AND b1=0 then …` answer a join, because the checker does not learn `b0 = 0` inside the arm: "Function body has type OR(Array1[\T,0,s0\],Array1[\T,b0,s0\])" (`:2421`, `:2432`, `:2795`). The ways are a checker rule that refines a size in the arm that tests it (no way of the six names it; 4e is the nearest), or the library's `cast` in the arm. No row.
- **Library slips, 10.** None waits on a design.
  - `__immutableFactory1` declares `ReadableArray1` where its callers need `ImmutableArray1` (`:2272`, `:2336`).
  - `__ImmutableSubArray1.put` calls a `put` that immutable arrays lack (`:2381`).
  - `mul`'s two local functions declare `()` and end in a parallel pair typed `((), ())` (`:2712`, `:2730`).
  - `TransposedMatrix` calls `add`, `subtract` and `negate`, which `Matrix` does not declare (`:2782` to `:2784`).
  - `SUFFIX_SUM`'s `seq((|x| - 2):0:-1)` passes a `Range[\ZZ32\]`, which no `seq` takes (`:4686`).
  - `matrix(v)`'s numeral `0` (`:2819`, row 437). Its repair's form follows fork 2: `v.zero` under a ring bound, the witness device under `Number`.
  - No row names the first nine.
- **The two export errors, 2** (`FortressLibrary.fss:12`).
  - The first lists 17 api declarations the component lacks. 14 are decision E's dead sizes, `DOT` and juxtaposition declared with size parameters they never use (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1650-1666`, `:1763-1793`), shown to him "with the switch-over's design" (POSITIONS, "Sizes."). The others are the two commented-out `immutableArray` ranks (`FortressLibrary.fss:2133-2138`) and `array3`.
  - The second is one error over about 50 traits, most of them not arrays (`Comparison`, `Range`, `String`, `Number`, `Maybe` among them). It clears only with the library-wide api match.

### Sites that need two forks, or a fork and something else
  - The 9 slips of section 1 (row 437's `:2819` waits on fork 2's form).
  - The `row` parameter types that unhide `Array2` and `Array3` (not among the 94).
  - These fit the planner's pile 1 ("decided and free to fix, the library's one-off slips", `PLAN.md:21`), if he agrees that the arrays' slips are not the array design. That is one line to ask.
- **Three groups need a list of ways first:** the 13 bodies typed by their parent trait, the 3 sizes tested in a branch, and the two export errors (decision E with the switch-over's design, and the library-wide api match).

## 4. The order now, and the first question

content.content:
# Planning the road

`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md` holds the phases, the questions for the curator in the order they are needed, and the parked items. Keep every open question there, in the order it needs deciding, and none only in your context.

**nine steps**
: Order in which a fork is answered from the evidence: (1) what the mathematics says; (2) what each path does today, measured; (3) what the specification says under every spelling; (4) what the library does in the same family; (5) where the designers departed from Java; (6) what peer languages and their implementations do; (7) what the commits say; (8) the derivation from the curator's principles in POSITIONS; (9) the decision, yours or the curator's (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions"). Steps 3, 5 and 7 give the team's word, step 4 the library, and step 6 the peers; the order sets no precedence. `SKILL.md` gives the peers their place.

**re-approval rows**
: Earlier decisions put to the curator again, parked in PLAN, "Off the path, parked".

## Procedures

- Ask for the curator's answers in PLAN's order, after you check each question against the three principles. Raise the re-approval rows and other parked items only when the work reaches them.
- If a probe can answer a known fork, run it while you plan, before the batch is briefed, so that the worker gets a task with the decision made. If the fork is consequential, put the probe's result to the curator as an ask.
- Answer each fork by the nine steps. Seek one global rule from type theory, and from the peers' implementations where the peers weigh (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions"), not a rule on a rule.
- Put re-approval rows to the curator one theme per message, each row in detail, with the ask's short primer (`SKILL.md`, "An ask", item 2) and what makes sense in a high-performance language. The count of reversals is not the measure.
- Give idle time to the parked research in PLAN. It needs no go, but a new deliverable does: discuss it with the curator before you make it.
- Park what needs the curator's machine; do not simulate it.

You list the ways for the array sites that remain in the distance, for a question the coordinator will put to the curator. You decide nothing.

## The problem

The distance is every error the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, 34 at climb batch 18's gate (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-18/gate/distance.txt`; the per-site list is `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`). It must reach zero before the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto that library, and a type error stops the compile of the component that holds it. 21 of the 34 are in the library's array code, all in the `FortressLibrary` component:

1. 14 method bodies of `Vector` and `Matrix` typed by their parent trait, such as "Function body has type Array1[\T,0,s0\], but declared return type is Vector[\T,s0\]", because `map`, `ivmap`, `fill` and `tabulate` are declared on the parent.
2. 3 sizes tested in a branch: `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => r` and `if b0=0 AND b1=0 then ...` answer a join, because the checker does not learn `b0 = 0` inside the arm.
3. Row 678's `Col` and `Row` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2697`, `:2701`).
4. The two export errors at `FortressLibrary.fss:12`: the first lists 17 api declarations the component lacks (14 of them `DOT` and juxtaposition declared with size parameters they never use, PLAN item 12; the two commented-out `immutableArray` ranks; `array3`); the second spans about 50 traits, most of them not arrays.

The record's diagnosis of these groups is `explorations/reviews/array-forks-now.md`, section "None of the six" and the lines after it, on the tree of 2026-10-09; take its findings as given, and check only that each site is still where it says (the per-site list above is today's). It found that no array fork clears any group, and that each group needs a list of ways first. The array forks and their ways are `explorations/reviews/array-design-ways.md`.

## What to do

For each of the four groups, list every way that the language and the library offer to clear it, the library's own way first: how the library already does the same kind of thing elsewhere, its devices (a redeclaration at the leaf's own type, `cast`, the witness `typecase`, a body built through `tabulate`), the specification's word, and the checker or walk change a way would need. Follow the order of the nine steps (the `coordinator` skill's `references/road.md`), steps 1 to 8; take no step 9. For each way give:

- what it edits (library text, the api, the checker, walk) and how many sites it clears, by reading;
- whether it needs one of the decisions that P-85 or P-55 holds open (below), a decision of the curator's that the record does not hold, or none;
- what it does to walk's values, to the team's tests and to microGPT's two programs (`explorations/run-c4/`), by reading;
- what it costs in rungs.

Then say, for each group, which ways need no decision of the curator's, which need one, and which decision. Mark every reading of yours as yours.

## Limits

- A climb batch is running on this machine and times the checker's count stage on its base build. So build nothing, run no suite and no count or distance stage, and touch no worktree but the main tree. If a way needs a fact that only a run gives, you may run a few small programs under walk or compiled from the main tree `/home/user/fortress`, each under `nice -n 19`, set up as the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "Setting up each call", says; name each as a measurement, with its command and output.
- Write `explorations/reviews/array-sites-ways.md`, with a header comment saying what it is, at which commit, and what was run. Commit nothing: the batch lands on `main` later. Return the note's text in your report as well.
- Keep every wait under 270 seconds.

## The entries you need, word for word

- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with array decisions A, B and D (PLAN item 13).** The three: a store per element type chosen by the factory, the size also kept as a field of the store, and a factory for a size known only at run time that returns the unsized `Array`. A is how `double[]` goes under a float vector, B where unboxed arithmetic happens, D sizes in the model's own types (P-87). Also open: why `RR64` and not `RR32`, since LLMs train at FP32 at most; the one reason given is the Python reference's float64 output. P-55 holds the forks taken before the switch-over.
- P-55 **A size may hold arithmetic, compared by its written form once numerals are folded (item 15, 15a with (b)).** The checker accepts a sum, difference, product or power in a size. `2 3` folds to `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. The class loader computes the value when it makes a class. A size name may equal a numeral, as the team's Q&A answers, so the `N[\0\]` arm of a `typecase N[\b0\]` is reachable. The library keeps the team's sizes written as products and sums. Two later array forks stand at defaults while his answers are pending: fork 3, a size known only at run time, at way 4a, where his reading of P-40 is asked; and fork 2, the bound of `Vector` and `Matrix`, at the two-trait bound (PLAN items 13 and 52).
- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.
- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** An operator in the model never becomes a function call to satisfy an overload check. Any repair that changes a model line is shown to him as a diff before it is built. Decision D, the sized signatures of the flat program C4's vocabulary, is such a diff (`reviews/decision-d-diff.md`); nothing of it is applied before PLAN phase 5.

## Your report

The note's path, its first section in a few lines, each group's ways that need no decision, the decisions the others need, any site that is not where the record says, and each measurement you ran.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

<tools-used-before-summary>Agent, Bash, Edit, Read, Skill, Workflow, Write, mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__get_session, mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__send_later</tools-used-before-summary>
Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   - **Before this stretch** (see the earlier summary):
     - Review the Haiku window and redo its writing and decisions critically, with Opus reviewers and one Fable pass.
     - Work the redo plan in `postmortem-2026-10-19-haiku/fable-judgement.md`: D.1 record fixes, D.2 Opus work, D.3 ten asks one per message.
     - The model check hook and the git-check switch.
     - The three pushes' allow rules.
   - **This stretch:**
     - Boot after compaction.
     - Answer his questions: where the asks are gathered; whether the cold reads were Haiku, and whether to revert their fixes.
     - Proceed with batch 19 on the standing go for phase 3.
     - Item 58: he took option 1 (E).
     - He pointed out that the array-sites ways probe can run in parallel with the batch.
   - **Latest instructions:**
     - "Hold asks until morning. I'm going to sleep now."
     - "Please try to NOT give me a wall off text for breakfast."
     - "also keep the running commentary when you do post batch landing review etc. to a minimum."
     - Then: "safe to compact you now?"

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **The coordinator skill's boot:**
     - step 0, the model check by `get_session`;
     - read FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX whole;
     - run check-index;
     - PLAN's first section, BOOT, HELD, git log;
     - batch.md's "While it runs" for a running batch.
   - **The batch workflow** (`climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual):
     - planner, then Fable review in place, then splice (`gen19.py`, `check19.js --write`, `workflow-scenarios.js`);
     - base build: `ant compileAll`, the library order's 5 jars, a walk test, `git status --porcelain` clean, a trial seed, an `old-fortress.sh` run;
     - launch with `args` `{base, baseBuild}` byte for byte;
     - resume with `resumeFromRunId` after a stop.
   - **The standing go:** a batch launches if no consequential question is open; overnight, defaults are taken and put on the review list.
   - **Agents at once:** the two-at-once cap is per Workflow run, not for Agent-tool workers.
   - **Quiet times:**
     - say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails;
     - reply "." alone at a check-in;
     - no running commentary while he is away.
   - **The record tools:**
     - `record.py add P --section ... FILE --from PATH#HEADING --by --note`, unnumbered;
     - `record.py check --base`;
     - `ledger.py add --section`.
   - **P-153 (contract E):** an integer `^` returns its own type; a negative exponent raises `IntegerOverflow`; base 0 raises `DivisionByZero`; ±1 exact; a fraction comes from a float or rational base.
   - **A type error stops the compile**, so the 21 array distance sites must clear before FortressLibrary can compile at the switch-over.

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - **`explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md`:** rewritten and updated several times. Latest `b5c96fbec`. Its state:
     - Running: batch 19, run `wf_2408885e-820`.
       - Launched 00:37 UTC as task `whov93xgu`.
       - Stopped by the VM restart at 00:41:01 UTC; resumed at 00:43 UTC as task `wyp3nwahq`.
       - args `{"base": "612869b4a2934caf40cd17a7afcf2ab149fc9252", "baseBuild": "/home/user/fortress-base19"}`.
       - About 3.2M and 3 hours.
     - Check-ins "Batch 19 check-in 1" to "5", at 01:22, 02:07, 02:52, 03:37 and 04:22 UTC. The fifth arms two more if the run is still going.
     - Ask 2 answered at 00:45 UTC: E, P-153.
     - Ask 3 held for evidence. The ways worker `a41125b44611e9121` has run since 00:52 UTC; output `explorations/reviews/array-sites-ways.md`, uncommitted.
     - Ask 4 next.
     - He went to sleep at 00:48 UTC: no ask before his next message.
     - His word at 00:54 UTC: no wall of text for breakfast. The morning message is a few lines; then one ask per message.
     - Owed: the two FACTS hand-overs from the item 58 judgement's section 9; the revival page's parts 5 and 6; the reorientation; row 584's note; old section citations.
     - Owed to the writer: `sources.md` naming his yes to the two rules; the held cleaning rule; flag 12.
     - Machine: next cap stop about 13:41 UTC; 4.7 GB free.
   - **`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md` and its history** (`d3b5b812d`). P-153 added in "Numbers":
     ```
     - P-153 **An integer raised to a negative power raises an error; a fraction comes from a float or rational base (contract E, item 58).** Each integer type's `^` answers its own type at every exponent: a negative exponent raises `IntegerOverflow` where the result is no integer, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code types an integer power by its integer at a signed exponent (P-26); overloads choose by type, and no type carries an exponent's or a numeral's sign, so the split is on the base, with the sign tested at run time as the library tests every sign-refined subset (P-80). Still to build: the integer powers so typed, with row 747's typed `fail` in `strToInt`, and the team tests `realArith`, `compoundArray` and `simpleExp` and two demos written with a float base (PLAN item 58).
     ```
   - **`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`:**
     - Item 58 is prefixed "**Answered at 00:45 UTC on 2026-10-20: E, after the Fable judgement ... (P-153); to build in a batch after 19.**"
     - Line 61 now reads "by item 58's answer, E (P-153; F-241)".
     - Line 13 and item 17 say batch 19's record is drafted and reviewed (`2d91166b8`).
   - **`explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`:** row 785 added (walk refuses a pair whose more specific declaration writes no return type), at `52f8bdffb`.
   - **`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-19.md`:** by the planner (`8cfe2638d`). I edited "The coordinator filed it as row 785"; the Fable reviewer fixed six slips (`e5f490b3c`).
   - **`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-19-review.md`:** the Fable review, verdict ready to launch.
   - **`explorations/reviews/integer-power-fable-judgement.md`:** committed with its INDEX line (`c302e4613`).
   - **`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js`:** manifest spliced (`612869b4a`).
   - **Scratchpad briefs** in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/haiku-window/`:
     - `brief-review19.md`;
     - `brief-arrayways.md`: the four groups of 21 array sites; read-only, `nice -n 19` small runs only; P-85, P-55, P-27 and P-87 word for word;
     - `row-noreturn.txt`;
     - `p-power.md`.
   - **Worktrees:**
     - `/home/user/fortress-base19`, the base build; rung P and its skeptic time the count stage there, so nothing else runs there;
     - the batch's `/home/user/fortress-existential` and `/home/user/fortress-stringconv`;
     - `/home/user/fortress-base-p152` removed;
     - the probe worktrees `fortress-probe-*` remain.

4. Errors and fixes:
   - **`old-fortress.sh`** ran without the setup lines and failed on the JDK version. Fixed by running the setup lines first: `JAVA_HOME` set to java-25, `unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`.
   - **`record.py add`** refused the "P-0" prefix. Removed it, and the tool numbered the entry P-153.
   - **The ways worker's start.** I first said it would start "when batch 19 frees a slot". The curator challenged this. The cap is the Workflow run's, so I admitted it and launched the worker at once.
   - **A boot-note rewrite dropped the FACTS hand-over line.** Added it back.
   - **A "00:5x" placeholder time** in the boot note was replaced with the clock's 00:47.

5. Problem Solving:
   - **Batch 19 prepared and launched.** It resumed after the VM restart with no rollback.
   - **The asks question** answered from D.3.
   - **The cold-read worry:**
     - both cold reads ran on Opus at 22:59 UTC, after the window;
     - all 11 since 2026-10-08 ran on Opus, and the writer is pinned to opus;
     - all 46 flags fall on changed lines (about 108 lines from `0707ac9ac^`);
     - no revert.
   - **Ask 3's framing found wrong.** The 21 array sites need no P-85 fork, per `array-forks-now.md`. A ways worker is running instead.

6. All user messages:
   - **On the cleaning pass:** "Word for word …when there are obvious typos, from using the slide keyboard mobile … is i hope still understandable by Fable, but next time maybe give that a cleaning pass?" (before this stretch; answered "Noted").
   - **His usage paste:** context 269.1K of 1M; session 24%; weekly all models 37%, Fable 7%.
   - **On the asks:** "Where are you gathering all the asks? Are these from the haiku post Mortem? Or prep for next batch? I thought the first was necessary for the second. Did I miss or misunderstand them (the asks you were hinting at pre-compaction)? Maybe you need archeology scout to gather the “ask” honeys you were dropping?"
