Climb batch 18 landed at `e51759f57` on `main`, with the gate green and microGPT's quick check at 7 of 7 in both programs. Its post-batch review, `explorations/reviews/batch-18-review.md`, was written on 2026-10-19, after the coordinator found it had been skipped. Batch 17's writer task ran before batch 17's review, so that review's points never reached the skill either.

## A. `fortress-repo`

1. Fold each rung's revival change into `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md`, in the form that file already uses. The changes are in `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-18/RECORD.md`, section "Revival changes, for the skill writer" (from line 238), for rungs X (`372b9bf6a`), K (`396e4ed8d`) and W (`5262a2412`).
   - Each entry is plain, and says what changed and what the team left.
   - Leave out the batch's decisions, the curator's words and the lists of items for him: those stay in the record and the review list.
   - The file has no sentence on conditional extension yet. Rung X's entry gives it one, as the merged-diff review and its repair corrected it: the conditions hold while the entry itself and the declaration's members are checked, and not while its other `extends` entries or its header are (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-18/REPAIR-review.md`; FACTS F-255).
2. Correct the sentences that batch 18's review lists as false or incomplete, in its section 6:
   - `revival-changes.md:148`, its last sentence;
   - `:189-192`, "Four cases are not built yet";
   - `:217`, "bounded as the binding is";
   - `:220`;
   - `:222`, for a `where` clause on an `extends` entry;
   - `:46`, for rows 779 and 780 and the rule names;
   - `compiler.md:39`.

   Take each correct text from the FACTS entry the review cites (F-26, F-252, F-253, F-255, F-256, F-257), not from your own reading.
3. Correct batch 17's points that are still false, from the same section 6:
   - `revival-changes.md:46` and `interpreter.md:38` say "every pair of generic declarations" is read on declared domains. Functional methods of a generic trait or object are still compared on their instances (F-26, F-252).
   - `revival-changes.md:148` says "on its declared domain". That holds only where exactly one of the two declared domains lies inside the other (F-26, F-253).
4. Change only what this task names.

## B. Two hooks the curator approved on 2026-10-19

Both are in `.claude/settings.json`.

1. **The model check,** `.claude/hooks/model-check.sh`, a Stop hook. Its header comment says what it does. After each turn of the coordinating session it reads the model of the last reply from the transcript. If that is neither Opus nor Fable, it blocks the stop with an alarm. The session must then:
   - make the alarm the first line of its reply;
   - send it as a push notification;
   - do no other work until the curator switches the model back or says to go on.

   The compaction hook's text now checks the model first.
   - In `.claude/skills/coordinator/SKILL.md`, "The boot", make this step 0, before step 1: check the serving model with the `get_session` tool and no session ID (its `session_context.model` and `external_metadata.last_served_model`); if it is neither Opus nor Fable, tell the curator before anything else.
   - Say there in one line that the model check alarms at every turn, and what the session does on its alarm.
2. **The git-check switch,** `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, run at every SessionStart and Stop. Its header comment says what it does: it gives the platform's git-check script its empty body whenever the launcher writes it again.
   - In `.claude/skills/cloud-container/references/hooks.md`, "The platform's git-check hook": say that the switch does this at every start, so the step by hand and its manual approval are needed no more.
   - Keep how to tell that the hook is on (`grep -c stop_hook_active`), and that the launcher's script is kept as `stop-hook-git-check.sh.orig`.
   - `stops.md:51`, "The git-check hook is back on", is false now: correct it.
   - In `coordinator`'s `SKILL.md`, the line at `:209`, "After each process stop, tell the curator in one line that the git-check hook is back on. …", is false now: take it out.
   - `SKILL.md:151`, "Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently", stays, for a turn the switch misses.

## C. Two rules of the curator's, for the coordinator skill's "Quiet times"

1. His rule of 19:57 UTC on 2026-10-16, in the coordinator's words on the held list (`explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`, line 7): "While he is away, the coordinator keeps its messages to the minimum, gathers evidence and does its work, and sends no running commentary or line he cannot act on." He called a closing line that offers queued questions "for whenever you want them" a teaser.
2. A line on the held list is never cited as his yes, in the record or to him: being on the list answers nothing (`HELD.md`'s header says so). A batch record cited a held line as his approval (`explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-10-19-haiku/fable-judgement.md`, section C, item 3).

Put each where it belongs in `SKILL.md`. Write it as the skill's other rules are written, and keep the part no longer than it needs to be.

Change nothing else in the `coordinator` skill. In particular, leave `SKILL.md:101-102`, the rule on changes to the coordinator's own skill, alone: it waits for the curator's answer.

## Checks and report

- Run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py` on each part you change before the commit.
- Commit on `main`, one commit for A, one for B and one for C. Push nothing.
- Your report:
  - each commit, with each edit in one line;
  - every sentence this task names that you could not find in the skill;
  - every place where a FACTS entry and this task disagree.
======
# Task: the four open points of task 18, ruled

Take each as written:

1. `coordinator` `SKILL.md:150`: cut the clause "or after a process stop the hook's one line". It pointed to the line on the git-check hook that you took out.
2. `SKILL.md:115`: say that the git-check switch turns the platform's git-check hook off at every start, so that the hook asks for a commit only on a turn the switch misses. Keep "Its reminders are advisory."
3. `SKILL.md:152`: add the model check's alarm to the times a push notification is sent.
4. `cloud-container` `SKILL.md:45`: "how to turn it off" becomes "how it is turned off".

On your two disagreements with the task: F-256's version of `:189-192` stands, and so do the rung W citations as you copied them. Add the lines for these four edits to the two skills' `sources.md`. Run the lint, commit on `main`, push nothing. Report the commit, with each edit in one line.

=====
# Task: the cold read's flags on the hooks and the two rules, ruled

A cold read of `coordinator`'s `SKILL.md` and `cloud-container`'s `SKILL.md`, `hooks.md` and `stops.md`, from `c3e2b8e1f` to `3c8b6d5e7`, gave 21 flags. The coordinator's rulings follow. Make each edit as ruled, in the part named, as the skill's other rules are written.

## `coordinator` `SKILL.md`

- **C1, line 115.** Take the cold read's text: "The git-check switch, `.claude/hooks/git-check-off.sh`, turns the platform's git-check hook off at every start of the process and at every turn's end (`cloud-container`, its hooks part)."
- **C2, line 115.** Replace "So the hook asks for a commit only on a turn that the switch misses" with: if a git-check reminder still comes, the switch missed that turn. Answer it as line 151 says.
- **C3, line 149.** Define "away": the curator has said that he is away or asleep, or the turn started from a check-in or a hook, not from his message.
- **C4, line 149 against line 102.** While he is away, a skill change's report waits until he is back, as one message.
- **C5, lines 151 and 211.** The model check's alarm holds over the quiet times' rules, the "." reply at a check-in included.

1:I fixed all 46 flags in one commit on `main`, `475be9b38`. The lint is clean, and nothing is pushed. Flag 12 is settled only in part, and two edits go a little beyond the flags; both are under "What to look at".
2-
3-**`revival-changes.md`, "Walk's check of two generic declarations"**
4-1. I added "Here `Round extends Shape` and `Circle extends Round`; `Wide` is any trait." The tests confirm this.
5-2. "Declared domain" is now defined once, at its first use: "the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept, at every instance within its bounds". I cut "each over its own instances", and the sentence is restated as "every pair of functions of which at least one is generic".

- Original: the traits chapter says that a type provides the method declarations it declares and inherits, and that it does not inherit one that its own `override` declaration overrides or whose parameter types its own declaration repeats. The compiled checker read every declaration of every supertype as provided, and refused the team's `ProjectFortress/tests/disp0.fss`, whose `override` widens a parameter.
- Resolution: both paths read what a type provides as the chapter says. The checker checks that the return type of an overriding declaration is a subtype of the return type of the declaration that it overrides.
- Reason: the specification's rule, which walk follows (above). The team's own test is valid by it.

**Abstract functional methods in the checker's overloading check**

**Ask 3: the vector products' unused sizes**

The api declares 14 vector and matrix products with sizes they never use. Which way should clear the error this gives?

**Context**
- A reminder: a `nat` is a size that the type carries, as `Vector[\RR64, 16\]` carries 16.
- The api writes `opr DOT[\T, nat n, nat m, nat p\](a: Vector[\T,n\], b: Vector[\T,n\]): T`. The `m` and `p` appear nowhere. The component, the code behind the api, writes `[\T, nat n\]`, which is right. The export check wants the two headers to be the same, so it reports all 14 as missing. The slip is the team's.
- Your decision on record: these unused sizes go only by a diff shown to you with the switch-over's design. That design is now: a type error stops `FortressLibrary` from compiling, so the switch-over needs the distance at zero.
- What goes into the next batch without an ask, as the library's own way, on your review list:
  - `Vector`'s `+` builds its result through its parent, `Array1`, so the checker sees an `Array1` where a `Vector` is declared. The library's `cast`, a checked type test, gives the result back its type, as the library's `array1` factory already does. It costs one test per operation, not per element.
  - `fill` and `tabulate` redeclared in `Vector` and `Matrix` at their own type, as the team redeclares `copy` and `map`.
- Measured by a probe: those take the distance from 31 to 12, with nothing new. Walk's 40 array tests and microGPT's quick check don't move.

**Options**
1. **The diff.** The api's 17 headers lose their unused sizes: the 14 products, and 3 vector `+` and `-` that the error doesn't list. Distance 12 to 11. It also clears 3 of C4's `DOT` errors on the compiled checker, so microGPT is closer to compiling. Api only; walk unchanged. The diff: https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch
2. **The component copies the slip.** Its 14 headers gain the unused sizes. Distance 12 to 11, the same sites. The slip then sits in two places, and C4's 3 `DOT` errors stay, since a call can't fix `m` and `p`.
3. **The export check ignores them.** A checker change, and a revision of the specification's rule that the two headers must be the same. Distance 12 to 11. C4's 3 errors stay.

**How they weigh:** 1 fixes the slip where it is, and costs you one read of a 17-line diff. 2 needs no read, but doubles the slip and leaves microGPT's errors. 3 bends the specification for a slip.

Default: 1, built in the next batch with the other array fixes.

Recommendation: 1.

## Part 3. Skill sentences the batch made false

For the skill writer. The gather's record names three, `revival-changes.md:56`, `:58` and `:61` at `ebd39a6bd` (`RECORD.md:202-207`), which `45a0ff799` rewrote. Lines below are of `.claude/skills/` at `f4c6fba1a`; `fortress-repo` has not changed since `45a0ff799`.

**Made false by batch 19, beyond those three:**
1. **`fortress-repo/references/interpreter.md:38`**: "For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it loads the pair only if the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the return-type rule hold on their declared domains." Walk loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which breaks the Meet Rule (row 788; `XXXGenericObjectInstanceBesidePlainWalk`, 'Saw expected failure: loaded and ran, not refused at load', `RECORD.md:30`). It was false on the base too; this batch measured and filed it. The sentence ends with a pointer to the departures; "except in the cases that it lists" makes it true.
2. **`fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md:57`**: "In seven cases, walk or the checker departs from these rules:". Row 787 is an eighth, made by rung P: walk refuses a pair whose parameter types exclude only together where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own, and the checker accepts it (F-258; `XXXGenericPairWhereExcludesTogetherWalk`). The writer put it at `:73`, under the new section's limits, not in this list. The boot note already gives it to the writer's next task.

**Not false, but now incomplete:**
- **`revival-changes.md:61`** (row 759): the checker accepts `g[\T\](a: T)` beside `g(a: Any)` only with the bound unwritten; with `T extends Any` written it refuses the pair (`K759A`, `rung-existential-reduction/SKEPTIC.md:106`; `changes.tex:2845-2851` since `b9711575b`). The measured cause: the compiled path bounds an unwritten type parameter by `Object` (row 412; `compiler.md:69`), so on that path the two domains are not equal.
- **`revival-changes.md:130-134`** ("An object or trait declared `extends Any`"): true as built; its reason cites the text's rule only, and it says nothing of the specification's own `Tuple` and algebraic roots (Part 1, split 1). It changes with gather.2's answer.
- **`fortress-repo/references/compiler.md:125`**, "about 1.5 minutes": the count stage took 61 to 75 s in this batch and 64 s at the gate (batch 18's review said the same).
- **`coordinator/references/batch.md:45`**: the first-turn share is 0 by the brief's order in batches 14 to 19; "it fell to 25 to 35" describes the batches before.

**Checked and not false:** `SKILL.md:123` and `:126`; `compiler.md:39` (a declaration with a `where` clause of its own refused by the code generator, which row 787's pair meets) and `:69`; `interpreter.md:84`; `gate.md:70` (the microGPT phases only are compared, which is why section 1's message move raised nothing); `session.md:55-63`; `coordinator`'s `delegating.md:53` (an unfinished agent runs from its start on its worktree's leftovers, as both resumed workers did); `cloud-container`'s `stops.md` on a VM restart with the disk intact; the writer's new sections on exclusion (`revival-changes.md:67-75`), on `||` (`:136-140`) and row 788's case (`:64`).

## After the landing: the coordinator's routing

The coordinator's steps after a landing, in this order, each done whole:

1. The landing report to the curator.
2. The routing: every open row, record default and item for the curator filed with a batch or as a parked line of `PLAN.md`. Each is checked against POSITIONS and the notes `INDEX.md` lists before it is called open, put to the curator or briefed. In the same pass the routing moves out of `PLAN.md` each item the batch built or answered, and any item it finds stale: word for word, into `PLAN-history.md`, under the landing's dated heading and the heading the item stood under. The batch's own line in its phase becomes one line, with its landing commit and its review. An open item whose text also stands in another home (a `review-queue.md` entry, a ledger row, a FACTS or POSITIONS entry) becomes one line in `PLAN.md`: what is asked, its default, and a pointer to that home. No other step takes an item out of `PLAN.md`, which held 519K characters before its consolidation of 2026-10-15, 54 % of them closed (`process-engineering/plan-map.md`, sections 2 and 4).
3. FACTS consolidated as its README says, superseded text moved to `FACTS-history.md`. The commit stage has already written the landed count and distance.
4. The skills, in three moves:
   - One task for the standing skill writer (`tools/skill-writer.sh`, its brief `skill-writer-brief.md`): the batch's revival-change material, the section "Revival changes, for the skill writer" of its `RECORD.md`; the skill sentences that the post-batch review lists as false; and any `skill-touched` item. The writer runs `tools/skills-lint.py` before each commit.
   - A cold read of the parts the writer changed, by an agent given only the skill and `skill-cold-read-brief.md`.
   - The writer fixes the cold read's flags, and the coordinator pushes its commits.
5. The next batch launched only after that, so that its workers read the updated skill (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The landing").
6. The combined post-batch review, started at the landing, since step 4 takes its list of false skill sentences (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The landing").

The review explains every new or risen row of the checker count by a named rung edit. It reads the microGPT walk check's result. It reports the batch's measures against the batches before it with `tools/batch-measures.py` on the run's directory (`batch-redesign.md`, "The measures").

### Climb batch 19, listed for his review

The items for him that climb batch 19's rungs, skeptics, gather and merged-diff review left (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-19/RECORD.md`, "Items for the curator"), one entry for each point, opening with the ids it holds. None blocks a batch or the switch-over; each is reversible, and each default is the one on record.

- P.worker.1 and P.skeptic.1 of climb batch 19's rung P: `tint` (row 786), the P-152 probe's question 1, is still open. Walk loads `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, reading two type parameters whose bounds exclude as never one type, and the compiled checker refuses it, 'Invalid overloading of tint'; `Bottom` lies within both bounds (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:583-584`) and cannot be written (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:106-107`), so which path moves is his. Default: both paths as they are, row 786 `CONTESTED` (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-19.md`, section 2, fork 3). Evidence: `ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairExcludingWalk.fss:23-24`; `mayBeEqual`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:1458`; `compile-ladder/rung-existential-reduction/REPORT.md:236`.

- gather.2 of climb batch 19's gather: the specification declares `trait Tuple extends Any excludes { Object }` (`Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:180-186`, trait `Fortress.Core.Tuple`) while its rule makes every trait but `Any` and `Object` extend `Object` implicitly (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:186-188`; `Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:159-160`), and rung S's desugaring follows the rule, leaving only `Any`'s and `Object`'s own declarations as written (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/desugarer/PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:123-124`). Neither library declares `Tuple`, so nothing reaches it today; a library that ships the specification's `Tuple` would see it made an `Object` against its own `excludes` clause. Should the rule and the desugaring name `Tuple` beside `Any` and `Object`? No default on record. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-string-conversion/SKEPTIC.md:94` (section 5); `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:423`, "Object extends Any alone and Tuple likewise".

- review-routed.1 of climb batch 19's merged-diff review, for the next batch that edits the checker's overloading code or its tests: row 789 (the compiled checker refuses an overlapping pair with 'V is not in the kind env' in place of 'Invalid overloading') is filed at home 3 with no reproducer, but a gated test can pass while it shows, so one is owed (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", home 3): a plain compiled test of the row's program, `compile` with `compile_err_contains=is not in the kind env`, seen passing through `junit.sh`, and named in the row once `ledger.py` has a route for a reproducer (review-queue item 165). Evidence: `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:460`; `compile-ladder/rung-existential-reduction/SKEPTIC.md` section 5.

- review-routed.2 of climb batch 19's merged-diff review, for the next batch that edits the checker's exclusion test or row 786: `tint` (row 786, `CONTESTED`) is home 3, and only walk's half is asserted (`ProjectFortress/tests/GenericPairExcludingWalk.fss:23-24`); the checker's refusal, 'Invalid overloading of tint', is in the row's notes and in no gated test. Owed: a plain compiled test of the pair, `compile` with `compile_err_contains=Invalid overloading of tint`, seen passing through `junit.sh`, so that a change of either path's reading turns a test red. Evidence: `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:459`; `compile-ladder/rung-existential-reduction/REPORT.md` section 11.

### Not classified, to check
## For the curator

In the order they need you, each with its default:

1. **An object or trait declared `extends Any` is now an `Object`, but the specification's own `Tuple`, and its algebraic roots such as `BinaryPredicate`, are declared `extends Any` to stand beside `Object`, so the text contradicts itself (gather.2).** Default (mine, none on record): as landed; name `Tuple` beside `Any` and `Object` when a library first declares it, and decide the algebraic roots with row 37.
2. **`tint` (row 786): walk loads two declarations whose type parameters' bounds exclude, and the checker refuses them.** Default: both paths as they are.
3. **`FlatString`'s api no longer declares `opr ||(a:FlatString, self)`, where climb batch 15's default kept it for your item 38 (review.1).** Default: as landed.
4. **Rung P's sentence in `overloading.tex` adds "or their elements at one position" to the words the record gave it, toward the type group's paper.** Default: as landed.
5. **The record's sixteen forks, taken at their defaults, and its points for your sight** (team lines changed in the checker's exclusion test, in `String`, in `FlatString`'s api and in the desugaring; walk's moved values for tuples and functions beside a string). Default: as landed.
6. **microGPT's APL port now stops at the same compile phase with a different first error, "DelegatedIndexed is undefined.", from rung S's `FlatString` api.** Default: as landed.

- The count stage took 64 s and the distance stage 153 s at the gate. Load explains the count's change; the distance's 20 s is inside the spread of same-code runs, not explained by load.
- The batch wrote 3.82M over 12 agents in 2 h 56 min, against the record's 3.2M and 3 hours. The VM restart cost 0.35M of it, and the review's judge and repair 0.41M. Preparation cost 1.60M more.

178. **The members of a conditional extension scoped to the condition (row 773).** The checker checks a member under a conditional extension's condition, as P-151 says. The member stays callable where the condition fails, since the members a type inherits are read at every instance: `Lst[\Fn\](Fn(inc), Fn(inc)).lt(...)` compiles, and its run dies at link time, 'NoSuchMethodError: ... CondExtendMember$Fn.lt(CondExtendMember$Fn)'. Swift, Rust and Haskell scope such members to the condition. The scoping waited on row 748's check at a dotted call, which rung K landed in the same batch; that check reads a method's own `where` clause only, so row 773 holds.

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

By the exclusion rule, a value of both declared domains has, at each position, only one instance of each generic type that the parameter types there are or extend. content.text:
**Ask 3: the vector products' unused sizes**

The api declares 14 vector and matrix products with sizes they never use. Which way should clear the error this gives?

**Context**
- A reminder: a `nat` is a size that the type carries, as `Vector[\RR64, 16\]` carries 16.
- The api writes `opr DOT[\T, nat n, nat m, nat p\](a: Vector[\T,n\], b: Vector[\T,n\]): T`. The `m` and `p` appear nowhere in it. The component, the code behind the api, writes `[\T, nat n\]`, which is right. The export check wants the two headers to match, so it reports all 14 as missing. The team made this slip.
- Your decision on record says these unused sizes go only by a diff shown to you with the switch-over's design. That design is due now. One type error stops `FortressLibrary` from compiling, so the switch-over needs the distance at zero.
- The other array errors need no ask. The next batch fixes them with devices the library already uses, and each goes on your review list:
  - `Vector`'s `+` builds its result through its parent, `Array1`. So the checker sees an `Array1` where a `Vector` is declared. The library's `cast` is a checked type test. It gives the result its `Vector` type back, as the library's `array1` factory already does. It costs one test per operation, not per element.
  - `fill` and `tabulate` are declared again in `Vector` and `Matrix`, at their own types. The team does the same with `copy` and `map`.
- A probe measured those fixes: the distance goes from 31 to 12, with no new errors. Walk's 40 array tests and microGPT's quick check don't change.

**Options**
1. **The diff.** The api's 17 headers lose their unused sizes: the 14 products, and 3 vector `+` and `-` that the error doesn't list. The distance goes from 12 to 11. It also clears 3 of C4's `DOT` errors on the compiled checker, so microGPT gets closer to compiling. Only the api changes; walk doesn't. The diff: https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch
2. **The component copies the slip.** Its 14 headers gain the unused sizes. The distance goes from 12 to 11, the same errors. The slip then sits in two places. C4's 3 `DOT` errors stay, because a call can't fix `m` and `p`.
3. **The export check ignores them.** This is a checker change, plus a change to the specification's rule that the two headers must be the same. The distance goes from 12 to 11. C4's 3 errors stay.

**How they compare:**
- Option 1 fixes the slip where it is. It costs you one read of a 17-line diff.
- Option 2 needs no read. But it doubles the slip and leaves microGPT's errors.
- Option 3 bends the specification to cover a slip.

**Default:** option 1, built in the next batch with the other array fixes.

**Recommendation:** 1.

content.content:
**Decision E2, concretely.** There is no `killNatIvars` and no default to 0. An unsolved nat
variable is simply left in place; `hasInferenceVars` was extended to find one, so an unknown
size that reaches a **type** is reported by the existing "not enough context" path
(`impls/Functionals.scala:248-250`), and one that reaches nothing is never looked at. That is
why the api's dead sizes pass: their parameters occur in no domain, no range and no body, so no
constraint about them is ever generated and no entry for them ever enters the solver.

The plan says six such declarations at `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1508-1523`. Measured, the
api has **25** declarations with at least one dead size, and the six with a dead `nat m, nat p`
are at `:1511, :1514, :1517, :1520, :1523, :1526` — the plan's line range is three lines early
and stops one short. The others: a dead `nat o` in the three `subarray` methods (`:1401`,
`:1423`, `:1451`) and two dead offsets in the 2-D one (`:1562`); a dead `nat m` in three vector
operators (`:1499-1505`); a dead `nat p` in eight matrix operators (`:1624-1646`); and a dead
`nat n` in four traits whose parameter is part of their identity (`:1068, :1089, :1091, :1093`).
Under E1 (default to 0) or E3 (delete them) the library edit would be 25 declarations, not six.

**What is deliberately not in.** The `checkP` relaxation of
`perf-probes/prelude/exclusion-trace.md` § 5 (landed 2026-09-21) is not here, so the library's
exclusion errors stay and the before/after counts are comparable. Exclusion between two nat
literals is also untouched (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:447-451`, "Todo: Handle int, nat, bool args"):
an overload set distinguished only by two sizes is still rejected as ambiguous, the
conservative side, and the team wanted it allowed (`internal-document.tex:183-198`). `bool`,
`dim` and `unit` get a named checker error, not rules. `where`-clause `NatConstraint`s and
`requires` contracts are untouched.

## 3. The probes (§ e step 2)

All in the **compiler's own world** — `CompilerLibrary` as the prelude — compiled into a private
cache that the shadow built from scratch in library order. Capture: `01-probes-shadow.out`;
`pNat1`'s run-time failure in full: `01b-pNat1-run-stack.out`.
```

and the same for `Array1`'s `subarray` at `:1451` against the same `:1401`.

**Those two are almost certainly wrong, and they are the shadow's own doing.** The api declares
`trait ImmutableArray1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\] extends { … ReadableArray1[\T,b0,s0\] }`
(`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1411-1413`), so `ImmutableArray1[\T,b,s\]` *is* a
`ReadableArray1[\T,b,s\]` by declaration, whatever `b` and `s` are — the return-type rule is
satisfied and the checker says it is not. The three `subarray` declarations are also the only
ones in that family with a dead size (`nat o`, § 2), which is suggestive but does not by itself
explain it: with `argsAlwaysEqual` the `o` is just as dead and the check passes. Reading did not
find the mechanism, and it is not fixed here. **This is the one thing in this report that must
be understood before the real edit lands**: the checker denies a subtyping the api declares
outright, which is a wrong answer and not a missing feature, and the shape it denies —
`X[\T,b,s\] <: Y[\T,b,s\]` where `X extends Y[\T,b0,s0\]` — is `Vector`'s, `Matrix`'s and
C4's.

variable is simply left in place; `hasInferenceVars` was extended to find one, so an unknown
size that reaches a **type** is reported by the existing "not enough context" path
(`impls/Functionals.scala:248-250`), and one that reaches nothing is never looked at. That is
why the api's dead sizes pass: their parameters occur in no domain, no range and no body, so no
constraint about them is ever generated and no entry for them ever enters the solver.

The plan says six such declarations at `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1508-1523`. Measured, the
api has **25** declarations with at least one dead size, and the six with a dead `nat m, nat p`
are at `:1511, :1514, :1517, :1520, :1523, :1526` — the plan's line range is three lines early
and stops one short. The others: a dead `nat o` in the three `subarray` methods (`:1401`,
`:1423`, `:1451`) and two dead offsets in the 2-D one (`:1562`); a dead `nat m` in three vector
operators (`:1499-1505`); a dead `nat p` in eight matrix operators (`:1624-1646`); and a dead
`nat n` in four traits whose parameter is part of their identity (`:1068, :1089, :1091, :1093`).
Under E1 (default to 0) or E3 (delete them) the library edit would be 25 declarations, not six.

**What is deliberately not in.** The `checkP` relaxation of
`perf-probes/prelude/exclusion-trace.md` § 5 (landed 2026-09-21) is not here, so the library's
exclusion errors stay and the before/after counts are comparable. Exclusion between two nat
literals is also untouched (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:447-451`, "Todo: Handle int, nat, bool args"):
an overload set distinguished only by two sizes is still rejected as ambiguous, the
conservative side, and the team wanted it allowed (`internal-document.tex:183-198`). `bool`,
`dim` and `unit` get a named checker error, not rules. `where`-clause `NatConstraint`s and
`requires` contracts are untouched.

## 3. The probes (§ e step 2)

All in the **compiler's own world** — `CompilerLibrary` as the prelude — compiled into a private
cache that the shadow built from scratch in library order. Capture: `01-probes-shadow.out`;
`pNat1`'s run-time failure in full: `01b-pNat1-run-stack.out`.
```

and the same for `Array1`'s `subarray` at `:1451` against the same `:1401`.

**Those two are almost certainly wrong, and they are the shadow's own doing.** The api declares
`trait ImmutableArray1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\] extends { … ReadableArray1[\T,b0,s0\] }`
(`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1411-1413`), so `ImmutableArray1[\T,b,s\]` *is* a
`ReadableArray1[\T,b,s\]` by declaration, whatever `b` and `s` are — the return-type rule is
satisfied and the checker says it is not. The three `subarray` declarations are also the only
ones in that family with a dead size (`nat o`, § 2), which is suggestive but does not by itself
explain it: with `argsAlwaysEqual` the `o` is just as dead and the check passes. Reading did not
find the mechanism, and it is not fixed here. **This is the one thing in this report that must
be understood before the real edit lands**: the checker denies a subtyping the api declares
outright, which is a wrong answer and not a missing feature, and the shape it denies —
`X[\T,b,s\] <: Y[\T,b,s\]` where `X extends Y[\T,b0,s0\]` — is `Vector`'s, `Matrix`'s and
C4's.

opr DOT[\ T extends Number, nat n, nat m, nat p\](
        me:Array2[\T,0,n,0,m\], other:Array2[\T,0,m,0,p\])
        : Array2[\T,0,n,0,p\] = do

          (* If this were atomic, we could parallelize j-partition. *)
          res.put(res.get(a,c) + pr, a, c)
    mm(0,n,0,m,0,p)
    res
  end
end

+- F-35 **The `FortressLibrary` api has 25 declarations with a dead size, a size parameter that occurs in no parameter type, return type or body.** They check clean (P-40). They stand in the oldest library in the history, of 2007-01-04 (`72ae6881b`), where the six vector forms, scalar ones included, carry the matrix product's `nat n, nat m, nat p` beside it, with no `where` clause; in 2008 Jan-Willem Maessen took them out of the component while fixing walk's unification ("tons of latent type bugs came out", `32153798d`), and the api kept them. Where the component omits the dead size, the export checker reports the api's declaration missing. Six vector `DOT` and juxtaposition operators have this shape, `[\T, nat n, nat m, nat p\]` in the api and `[\T, nat n\]` in the component, and give one of the distance's export errors (F-53). P-40 lets the dead sizes go only by a diff shown to the curator with the switch-over's design. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 7.

- F-36 **The code generator's `FnNameInfo.boundsFor` gives a size parameter a size argument, and every other kind a type argument.** A `bool`, `dim`, `unit` or `opr` parameter still gets a type argument, a latent defect; the checker refuses the first three by name (F-67). A size symbol stays in the mangled name and needs no descriptor. Only a literal size reaches the class loader, which takes its descriptor from `RTTIsize.of` (F-129). Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` sections 1 to 3.

- F-37 **The one library's own sizes are the literals 0 to 3, and a compiled `typecase` on a size tests the value's own class.** A `typecase` tells `Vec[\ZZ32,3\]` from `Vec[\ZZ32,4\]` compiled by one `INSTANCEOF`, also when the size is a static parameter. A `typecase` that is a whole function body, with clauses that need a coercion, fails in code generation, size or not (row 340). Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRtCase` and `NatRtCaseGen`. Detail: `reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md` section 5; `perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md` section 4.

- F-38 **The compiled dispatcher chooses an overload arm generic in a size by the value's size, and the arm reads its size.** Called with an argument typed `Any`, the dispatcher reads the size off the value's descriptor. The checker's return-type rule compares the arms' own sizes (row 410). The dispatcher skips the bound `Object` that the compile path gives a size parameter (row 412). Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRtDisp`, `NatRtDispSize` and `NatRtDispTrait`. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/size-probes.md` section 2.

content.text:
You're right that it has an origin. In the git history it looks like a copied header, not a planned `where` clause. Here's what the history shows:

- **2007-01-04, the oldest library in the repository** (`72ae6881b`; nothing older is in git). The matrix product needs three sizes. `Matrix[\T,n,m\]` times `Matrix[\T,m,p\]` gives `Matrix[\T,n,p\]`, so its header is `[\T, nat n, nat m, nat p\]`. Right beside it, the six vector forms carry exactly the same header. Two of them are a vector times a scalar, which involve only one size. None has a `where` clause.
- **No `where` clause was needed.** The equality you have in mind is written by reusing the name. `DOT(me: Vector[\T,n\], other: Vector[\T,n\])` already says the two lengths are equal, because both say `n`. So `m` and `p` have no job in the vector forms. My reading: the header was copied from the matrix product.
- **2008-04-27, the team fixed it halfway** (`32153798d`). Jan-Willem Maessen fixed walk's type unification, and that fix brought out "tons of latent type bugs". In the same commit he cut the vector forms down to `[\T, nat n\]` and the matrix-vector forms to `[\T, nat n, nat m\]`. He did that in the component only. The api still had 18 such headers then, and they stayed.
- **Why nobody noticed:** walk runs the component and doesn't compare it with the api. The compiled checker's export check does compare them. But until the revival, it never checked this library, only the compiler's own.

So it's a slip with a history: a copied header that the team's own author later took out of the component, missing the api. I've added this to the record, in the facts entry on the api's unused sizes (F-35).

It changes ask 3 in one way. Option 1 now finishes the team's own 2008 fix, which is their later word on this. My recommendation is still 1. Is that your answer, or do you want to look at it again in this light?

That background task was my search of the old git history, for where the unused sizes came from. It has finished now, so your app showed it correctly.

Sorry, my last message was too compressed. Here is where we are.

**The goal right now**
- The compiled path must take over the interpreter's library. That step is the switch-over. Before it, the compiled checker must report no error on that library.
- The "distance" is the number of errors it still reports.
- Overnight, batch 19 took the distance from 34 to 31.
- The numbers 1, 6, 3 and 1 in my last message counted the errors that would be left, sorted by cause.

**The 31 errors left, by cause**
- 21 are in the array code. Your answer to ask 3 this morning unblocks them.
- 6 are in the integer power, `^` on integers, as in `2^(-1)`. It has nothing to do with arrays. You decided it last night: a negative power raises an error.
- 3 come from one checker defect. The checker refuses a reduction such as `SUM` when nothing at the call fixes its element type. This is checker work, and nothing needs deciding yet.
- 1 is in the combined `SUM` with `MAX`, an open item.

**The plan**
1. **Batch 20:** the array fixes with your diff, and the integer power. Both are decided. By the probe, the distance would go from 31 to about 5. I'm starting its planning now. It runs on your standing go for phase 3, so it needs nothing more from you.
2. **The asks.** The review of the Haiku window found ten decisions that were taken without you. They come to you one at a time. Asks 1 to 3 are done; asks 4 to 10 remain. None of them blocks batch 20.
   - Ask 4 decides one held item: walk's half of conditional extension. If you take it, it adds work to a later batch.
   - Ask 5 decides how the checker treats overloads of operators such as `+`. It matters later on the way to the switch-over.
   - Asks 6 to 10 are about how we work, plus a review of two decisions that already landed.

**Your time**
- Each ask takes about 5 to 10 minutes to read and answer.
- Nothing needs you before you drive.

Shall I send ask 4 now, or when you're back?

content.text:
You're right, and I said it wrong. "A negative power raises an error" is only one case of what you chose.

**The integer power, as you decided it** (your yes at 00:45 UTC, 02:45 your time)

The split is on the base's type, not on the exponent:
- An integer base gives an integer: `2^3` is `8`.
- If the true result is no integer, it raises an error: `2^(-1)` raises `IntegerOverflow`, since 1/2 is not an integer.
- Where the result is an integer, it is exact: `1^(-5)` is `1`, and `(-1)^(-3)` is `-1`.
- `0^(-1)` raises `DivisionByZero`.
- A float or rational base gives the fraction: `2.0^(-1)` is `0.5`.

Why the split is on the base: Fortress types have no sign. So no overload can tell `10^16` from `10^(-16)` by type, but one can tell an integer base from a float base. Your words at the time were "split on the base instead of the exponent". In the library, three team tests change from `10^(-k)` to `10.0^(-k)`.

**What the asks are, and what your answers changed**

The review of the Haiku window found things that happened without your informed yes, and turned each into one ask. They come in four kinds:
- **Work that was killed and needs a go** (ask 1). You said yes, and the digest and the cost tally ran.
- **Questions that were asked badly, or never asked** (asks 2, 3, 5). Your answers made new decisions. They didn't just agree with Haiku:
  - Ask 2 gave the power rule above.
  - Ask 3 gave this morning's diff. The review's default for ask 3 turned out wrong, so the probe changed the question.
- **Choices that landed in batches and were never put to you as choices** (asks 4, 7, 8). For each, you either keep what landed, which is the default, or order a change.
- **How we work** (asks 6, 9, 10).

So far, your answers have built new decisions. None of them just confirmed Haiku. Ask 4 is the first of the "keep or change" kind.

content.text:
**Ask 4: should a list of floats have a `<`?**

When a list's elements are only partly ordered, as floats are, should the list still get a lexicographic order?

**Context**
- **A lexicographic order** compares two lists element by element, like words in a dictionary: `⟨1, 5⟩ < ⟨2, 0⟩`.
- **Conditional extension** (P-151, built in batch 18): a trait can extend another only where a condition holds. The library now says:
  `List[\E\] extends LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`
  So a list gets `<` only where its elements are totally ordered.
- **Floats are only partly ordered,** because NaN compares with nothing. `QQ` is the same, because of 0/0. So the checker now refuses `⟨1.0, 2.0⟩ < ⟨1.0, 3.0⟩`. Integer and string lists keep their `<`.
- **Tuples work differently** (item 43, already built): a pair of floats does get a partial order. So `(1.0, 2.0) < (1.0, 3.0)` is accepted, and the same values in a list are refused.
- **The team's earlier text** points to a partial order for lists. The specification says a lexicographic order "may be partial or total depending on whether the ordering of the elements is partial or total". It also says lists compare when their elements support the comparison.
- **The team's later code** points to a total order only. Their unfinished advanced library bounds both of its lexicographic traits by a total order.
- **The 2012 library** gave every list an order, and walk still does (row 774).
- **The peers split:** Rust orders a vector of floats partly; Haskell and Scala order a sequence only over a total order; Swift gives arrays no order at all.
- **What it touches:** it doesn't block batch 20, and microGPT uses no `List`. The answer decides walk's half of conditional extension, a later batch's work.

**Options**
1. **As landed.** Lists are ordered only over totally ordered elements. A later batch then makes walk agree, so a list of floats loses `<` under walk too. The specification's sentence gets a revision note. Appendix I already names this departure.
2. **A partial order for lists too.** A second conditional entry, under `StandardPartialOrder`, gives lists of floats a partial lexicographic order. The library has no such trait yet, so this means designing one. It also needs a probe of whether one type can extend two conditional instances of the same trait. Walk's half comes after.

**How they compare:**
- Option 1 is built, and it follows the team's later code. It leaves a small mismatch: pairs of floats are ordered, but lists of floats are not.
- Option 2 restores the specification's sentence and matches tuples. It costs a probe and a new library trait, and it goes against the team's later code.

**Default:** 1, as landed.

**Recommendation:** 1. The team's later word outweighs its early text (P-26), and option 2 would add a trait the team never wrote.

content.text:
I delegated the heavy work: since the compaction, ten workers did the batch, the probes, the review, the cold read, the skill writer's tasks and the planning. Your question still has a fair point, though. I measured what entered my context since the compaction at 01:00 UTC, from the session's transcript:

1. **A harness reminder: about a third of everything since the compaction, by stored size.** About every 15 to 20 minutes, the harness pastes in a list of 217 old to-do items. The batch workers left them there, such as "Skeptic P19: fixes, SKEPTIC.md". It has done this 22 times since the compaction, about 1.3M characters as stored. I can't see exactly how many tokens each copy costs.
2. **The boot reads, about 100K tokens.** After a compaction, the boot reads the record whole. The note index (INDEX) alone is about 57K tokens; the facts file (FACTS) is about 34K.
3. **My own work, about 100K tokens.** Command outputs, about 60K; the scripts and briefs I wrote, about 33K; and reading the 51K-character array-sites note whole, to write ask 3.

The things I did myself were small but added up: the planning file's updates after the landing, the record's edits, and the git search for your question about the unused sizes.

Three fixes, biggest first:
- **Clear the 217 stale to-dos.** A small worker can delete them, and that stops the biggest drain. I'll do it now unless you say no.
- **Your call: read only the index's last 60 lines at boot,** and search the rest when needed. This is my proposal from 2026-10-16, still waiting on you. It saves about 50K tokens at each compaction.
- **Give the planning file's updates after a landing to a worker,** instead of doing them myself.

After the cleanup, compacting is a good idea.

# Running and reviewing a batch

The batch workflow is `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual, `climb-batch-workflow.md` beside it. Its stages run in this order: the scatter of the rungs, the rung workers, the skeptics, the judges and the repair round, the gather, the merged-diff review, the gate, and the commit stage. Read a stage's section of the manual when you reach it: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#<heading>'`.

**batch record**
: `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<name>.md`, written by the planner before the launch. Its rung sections are the workers' briefs; its other sections are for the curator.

**base**
: Commit that the batch starts from.

**gather**
: Stage that merges the rungs and folds their reports and record lines into the tree.

**merged-diff review**
: Review of the gathered diff, beside the gate, of the records, the reserved points and the routing.

**repair round**
: One round of fixes after the merged-diff review or the gate.

**commit stage**
: Last stage, which commits the landed tree and runs the pass of `references/record.md`.

**reserved point**
: Point that a batch record keeps for the curator, such as a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, or an interpreter output that a rung cannot explain.

**checker count**
: Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.

**distance**
: All the checker's errors on that library, which must reach zero before the switch-over: the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library.

## The go

- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.

## The workflow

- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
- At each landing, report the share of briefed agents that read the briefing at all. Aim for all of them. By the brief's order, none reads it in its first turn.

## The roles

- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, the skeptic also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", gives a reviewer. That run is the one exception to this bullet and to the rule that no stage measures a code state again.
- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.

## The checker count and the distance

The gate reports the checker count in every batch, and the distance in phase 3. Neither turns the gate red.

- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.

## Reserved points and repairs

- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.

## While it runs

- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the boot note, and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.

## The landing

1. Check that the commit stage folded the batch's entries into FACTS (`references/record.md`, "The pass").
2. Have the writer update `fortress-repo`'s `references/revival-changes.md` (`references/skill-rewrite.md`).
3. Name each decision that landed in one line, and put the items for the curator on the review list.
4. Have one Opus reviewer, which only reads, check the landed changes against the decisions on record and the library's way; measure misses by kind, the briefing's use and cost, and re-measuring; and run the routing check (the manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing").
5. File what the review finds in PLAN. Then make these moves yourself. The manual's section "After the landing: the coordinator's routing" gives `PLAN-history.md`'s heading for each landing and the form of the one line.
   - Move word for word into `PLAN-history.md` each item that the batch built, each question that the batch or the curator answered, and each stale item. A stale item is one that a decision or a landed change has made moot.
   - If another home holds an open item's whole text, cut it in PLAN to one line with a pointer there. If it holds part, first move the rest there. This holds for the review lists too: an entry that `review-queue.md` holds becomes such a line.
   - Repoint each citation of a moved item: `git grep -n 'PLAN\.md' -- explorations/coordinator/*.md explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md .claude/skills`. Cut a built item's part from its POSITIONS entry with `record.py`.

skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/fortress/.claude/skills/cloud-container

# The cloud container

**container**
: Virtual machine with its own disk, on which a cloud session of Claude Code runs. It holds a clone of the branch that the session was created from.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**main session**
: Top-level session of a container, which the curator talks to. The agents that it launches are not main sessions.

**coordinating session**
: Main session that keeps the project's files under `explorations/coordinator/` and launches the workers.

**process stop**
: End of the session's Claude Code process, by the platform's cap, by idleness or by a VM restart. The platform starts the process again in the same session.

**VM restart**
: Restart of the container's machine under a live session.

**check-in**
: One-shot reminder, armed with `send_later`, that wakes the main session with a message at a set time.

**Stop hook**
: Command that Claude Code runs at the end of every turn of the main session.

The platform stops the session's process about every 13 hours and when the session goes idle. It can restart the VM, sometimes with the disk rolled back, and it can lose the container. Running agents survive none of these.

## Rules for every agent

- Before a long run, read the room left on the disk as `references/machine.md` says.
- If your brief lets you push, push your work as you go, as `fortress-repo`'s `references/committing.md` says. Only what is pushed survives a rollback of the disk or a lost container.
- After a process stop, a VM restart or a lost container, run `git status` and `git log origin/<branch>..<branch>` in each tree that you work in, before you start anything again.
- The platform's git-check Stop hook can still ask the main session to commit and push on a turn that the git-check switch misses (`references/hooks.md`). Treat its reminders as advisory. Never commit or push unready work to answer one.

## The parts

- `references/machine.md`, for every agent: the machine, timings across sessions, agents at once, the disk allowance and a full disk, the blocked hosts.
- `references/stops.md`, for every agent: the kinds of process stop and their signs, a disk rolled back, the weekly usage limit, what a stop keeps here. Its section on check-ins is for the coordinating session.
- `references/hooks.md`, for the coordinating session: the transcript backup and its blind spots, the git-check hook and how it is turned off.
- `references/container-loss.md`, for the coordinating session: re-provisioning, re-arming the backup, reading another session's transcript, recovering the work.

How a Claude Code session behaves anywhere (the Bash tool, long commands, waits and the prompt cache, interrupts, the automatic permission check) is `fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md`. Running agents and resuming a run are the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font on an off-white ground, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding: a bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it. Pin every library URL to an exact version (`react@18.3.1` on jsDelivr or unpkg, `react/18.3.1/…` on cdnjs, `cdn.tailwindcss.com/3.4.17`), never a bare name, a range or a tag (`react`, `react@18`, `@latest`). Choose a version at least two weeks old. Any version you knew before this conversation is old enough; if you look versions up, skip any published in the last two weeks. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. The viewer never shows `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()` dialogs — `confirm()` returns false and `prompt()` returns null immediately — so build any confirmation step into the page itself.

**What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. Camera, microphone, screen capture, location, motion, Web Share and similar device APIs are refused without a prompt — build on one only when this user has a runtime capability for that device (the `artifact-capabilities` skill lists them) and the page declares it; otherwise take photos, audio and data as uploaded files instead (file inputs, drag-and-drop of files and `FileReader` work in browsers). A screen wake lock may be granted while the page is visible: request it and tolerate rejection. Fullscreen and pointer lock work from a click in desktop browsers; treat both as optional (handle the rejection) since phones and some app views lack them. Sound plays only after the viewer interacts (muted autoplay is fine), so start audio from a button. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#anchor` (letters, digits, `.` `_` `~` `-`) from the artifact's link reaches `location.hash` — never `#key=value` state and never the query string — so deep-link to a tab or section with a bare token and keep all other state in the page.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value
